items.stem: A clinician passively forward-flexes the patient's shoulder to 90° with the elbow bent to 90°, then passively internally rotates the shoulder. Which test is being performed?
options: Hawkins-Kennedy test
Neer test
Empty can (Jobe) test
Drop arm test
items.explanation: That position-and-motion combination — 90° flexion, elbow 90°, forced passive internal rotation — is the Hawkins-Kennedy test. A positive is reproduction of the patient's anterior/lateral shoulder pain. It is traditionally grouped with the 'impingement' tests, but a positive does not localize pathology to a specific structure.
items.pearl: Neer = passive full elevation with the scapula stabilized; Hawkins-Kennedy = flexion 90° + internal rotation. Examiners mix these up constantly.
items.citation: Cook C, Hegedus EJ. Orthopedic Physical Examination Tests: An Evidence-Based Approach. 2nd ed. Pearson; 2013 (test description).

items.stem: A patient places the dorsum of their hand against the mid-lumbar spine and is asked to lift the hand away from the back. Which muscle is this test primarily assessing?
options: Subscapularis
Supraspinatus
Infraspinatus
Teres minor
items.explanation: This is the lift-off test, described by Gerber and Krushell for isolated subscapularis rupture. Inability to lift the hand off the back — or compensating by extending the elbow or trunk — is a positive. The test is only valid if the patient has enough passive internal rotation to get the hand there comfortably in the first place.
items.citation: Gerber C, Krushell RJ. Isolated rupture of the tendon of the subscapularis muscle. J Bone Joint Surg Br. 1991;73(3):389-394.

items.stem: During active abduction a patient reports pain roughly between 60° and 120°, with less pain below and above that range. This finding is best described as:
options: A painful arc, associated with subacromial structures
A high painful arc, associated with the acromioclavicular joint
A capsular pattern of restriction
A positive drop arm sign
items.explanation: Pain through the mid-range of abduction (conventionally ~60-120 degrees) implicates the subacromial structures being compressed under the acromion, whereas pain confined to the top of range (commonly given as ~140-180 degrees) points to the acromioclavicular joint. A capsular pattern is a restriction of passive motion, not an arc of pain.
items.citation: Kessel L, Watson M. The painful arc syndrome. Clinical classification as a guide to management. J Bone Joint Surg Br. 1977;59(2):166-172 (syndrome and lesion classification). The specific degree boundaries above are textbook convention, e.g. Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment. 6th ed. Elsevier Saunders; 2014 - they are not stated as cut-offs in the 1977 paper.
items.contestedNote: The painful arc concept is well established, but the exact degree boundaries vary between textbooks (mid-range commonly 60-120 degrees; high arc quoted anywhere from 140 to 180 degrees). Treat them as descriptive conventions rather than validated cut-offs.

items.stem: With the patient's arm relaxed at the side, the examiner applies inferior traction and a visible depression appears just below the acromion. Name the finding.
options: Sulcus sign
Positive load-and-shift test
Hill-Sachs lesion
Positive jerk test
items.explanation: A sulcus sign — inferior translation of the humeral head producing a gap under the acromion — suggests inferior capsular laxity and is classically associated with multidirectional instability, the population Neer and Foster described the inferior capsular shift for. Interpret with symptoms: laxity alone is common in asymptomatic shoulders and is not the same as instability.
items.pearl: Laxity is a finding; instability is a diagnosis. The sulcus only matters if it reproduces the patient's problem.
items.citation: Neer CS 2nd, Foster CR. Inferior capsular shift for involuntary inferior and multidirectional instability of the shoulder. J Bone Joint Surg Am. 1980;62(6):897-908.

items.stem: Order the steps for performing the Hawkins-Kennedy test.
orderedOptions: Seat the patient with the arm relaxed and explain what you will do
Passively forward-flex the shoulder to 90° with the elbow flexed to 90°
Passively internally rotate the shoulder through available range
Ask whether their familiar pain was reproduced and compare to the other side
items.explanation: Setup, position, provocation, interpretation. The provocation is passive internal rotation from the 90/90 position — letting the patient actively rotate, or starting from an unstandardized position, changes what the test provokes.
items.citation: Cook C, Hegedus EJ. Orthopedic Physical Examination Tests: An Evidence-Based Approach. 2nd ed. Pearson; 2013 (test description).

items.stem: Order the steps of the apprehension–relocation sequence for suspected anterior instability.
orderedOptions: Position the patient supine with the shoulder at the edge of the table
Abduct the shoulder to 90° and flex the elbow to 90°
Slowly externally rotate toward end range while watching for apprehension or guarding
Keeping the arm in place, apply a posteriorly directed force over the humeral head
Note whether the apprehension eases with the posterior force (positive relocation)
items.explanation: Apprehension first, then relocation while still in the provocative position. The supine position lets the table stabilize the scapula and the examiner control rotation gently. Apprehension — not pain — is the response you are watching for at step 3, and its relief with posterior pressure is what makes the relocation informative.
items.citation: Cook C, Hegedus EJ. Orthopedic Physical Examination Tests: An Evidence-Based Approach. 2nd ed. Pearson; 2013; criterion detail per Farber AJ, et al. J Bone Joint Surg Am. 2006;88(7):1467-1474.

items.stem: Order the steps for goniometric measurement of shoulder external rotation at 90° of abduction.
orderedOptions: Position the patient supine with the shoulder abducted to 90° and the elbow flexed to 90°
Center the goniometer fulcrum over the olecranon process
Align the stationary arm perpendicular to the floor and the moving arm along the ulna toward the ulnar styloid
Passively rotate into external rotation while maintaining 90° of abduction
Read the angle at the firm end of range
items.explanation: Standard goniometric sequence: position, fulcrum, alignment, motion, measurement. Supine positioning helps stabilize the scapula and trunk; letting abduction drift or the trunk arch inflates the apparent rotation.
items.citation: Norkin CC, White DJ. Measurement of Joint Motion: A Guide to Goniometry. 5th ed. F.A. Davis; 2016 (shoulder lateral rotation procedure).

items.stem: Order the steps for a valid lift-off test.
orderedOptions: Confirm the patient has enough pain-free passive internal rotation to place the hand behind the back
Have the patient place the dorsum of the hand against the mid-lumbar spine
Ask the patient to lift the hand away from the back without extending the elbow or trunk
Grade inability to lift off, or compensation, as a positive test
items.explanation: The validity check comes first: a patient who cannot reach the position because of stiffness or pain cannot produce an interpretable lift-off, and many painful shoulders fail here. Watch for the classic cheats — elbow extension and trunk lean — which produce apparent lift-off without subscapularis activation.
items.citation: Gerber C, Krushell RJ. Isolated rupture of the tendon of the subscapularis muscle. J Bone Joint Surg Br. 1991;73(3):389-394.

items.stem: Across studies, the external rotation lag sign is consistently reported as highly specific (~98–100%) for full-thickness posterosuperior cuff tears, while its sensitivity varies widely (~56–97%) with tear size. Which statement best reflects its clinical role?
options: A positive strongly rules the tear in; a negative still leaves meaningful probability — especially for smaller tears
A negative definitively excludes a full-thickness tear
The test is clinically useless because sensitivity is inconsistent
It is primarily a test of subscapularis integrity
items.explanation: Specificity near 100% means false positives are rare — a clear lag is close to confirmatory (SpPin). Sensitivity depends on how much cuff is gone: small isolated supraspinatus tears often show no lag (~56% sensitivity), while extensive posterosuperior tears almost always do (~97%). So a negative mainly reassures against a LARGE tear; it cannot exclude a small one. Subscapularis has its own lag sign (internal rotation lag).
items.citation: Hertel R, Ballmer FT, Lombert SM, Gerber C. Lag signs in the diagnosis of rotator cuff rupture. J Shoulder Elbow Surg. 1996;5(4):307-313; Castoldi F, Blonna D, Hertel R. External rotation lag sign revisited: accuracy for diagnosis of full thickness supraspinatus tear. J Shoulder Elbow Surg. 2009;18(4):529-534.
items.contestedNote: Reported sensitivity ranges from ~56% (isolated supraspinatus) to ~97% (extensive tears) depending on study and tear extent; specificity is consistently high (~98–100%).

items.stem: Pooled estimates for the Hawkins-Kennedy test are roughly sensitivity 79% / specificity 59%. Used alone, what is it actually good for?
options: A negative modestly lowers the probability of subacromial pain; a positive localizes poorly
A positive confirms subacromial impingement
A positive confirms a rotator cuff tear
Nothing — it should never be performed
items.explanation: With Sn 79%/Sp 59%, the negative likelihood ratio is ~0.36 — a negative shifts probability down modestly — while LR+ is only ~1.9, so a positive barely moves the needle and certainly cannot identify which structure hurts. It earns its place in clusters, not as a standalone verdict.
items.citation: Hegedus EJ, et al. Which physical examination tests provide clinicians with the most value when examining the shoulder? Update of a systematic review. Br J Sports Med. 2012;46(14):964-978.
items.contestedNote: Pooled accuracy estimates vary across meta-analyses, and the 'subacromial impingement' construct itself is disputed — current terminology prefers rotator-cuff-related shoulder pain (RCRSP). Structure-specific claims for this test are not supported.

items.stem: In Farber et al.'s study of traumatic anterior instability, the apprehension test reached specificity ~96% — but only when which response was counted as positive?
options: Apprehension or guarding
Pain
An audible click
Loss of external rotation range
items.explanation: The positive criterion is the psychometrics. Using apprehension as the criterion, the test performed strongly (Sn ~72%, Sp ~96%); using pain, accuracy dropped substantially, because painful shoulders of many causes hurt in abduction–external rotation. If you call a merely painful apprehension position 'positive', you will over-diagnose instability.
items.pearl: Same maneuver, different positive criterion, different test. Record WHAT response you observed, not just '+ apprehension test'.
items.citation: Farber AJ, Castillo R, Clough M, Bahk M, McFarland EG. Clinical assessment of three common tests for traumatic anterior shoulder instability. J Bone Joint Surg Am. 2006;88(7):1467-1474.

items.stem: For diagnosing subscapularis tears, which pairing of test properties is correct (per Barth et al.)?
options: Bear-hug: more sensitive (~60%); lift-off: nearly perfectly specific but very insensitive
Lift-off: highly sensitive; bear-hug: highly specific
Both tests are highly sensitive screens
Both tests have poor specificity
items.explanation: Barth et al. reported the bear-hug as the most sensitive subscapularis test (60%), with specificity 91.7%, while the lift-off was positive in only 17.6% of tears but essentially never falsely positive (specificity 100%). So: bear-hug is the better screen (and still misses 4 in 10 tears — most subscapularis tears are missed clinically); a positive lift-off is close to confirmatory.
items.citation: Barth JRH, Burkhart SS, De Beer JF. The bear-hug test: a new and sensitive test for diagnosing a subscapularis tear. Arthroscopy. 2006;22(10):1076-1084.

items.stem: The Spurling test carries sensitivity ~30% and specificity ~93% for cervical radiculopathy. A patient with lateral shoulder and arm pain has a negative Spurling. Best conclusion?
options: Cervical radiculopathy is NOT ruled out — the test misses most cases
The neck is cleared as a pain source
The pain must be coming from the rotator cuff
The test should be repeated with more overpressure until positive
items.explanation: Sensitivity of ~30% means roughly 7 of 10 radiculopathies produce a negative Spurling — it cannot rule out. Its value runs the other way: with specificity ~93%, a positive that reproduces the patient's arm symptoms substantially raises the probability of a cervical source in a shoulder-pain presentation.
items.pearl: Every shoulder examination includes a cervical screen — precisely because no single negative test clears the neck.
items.citation: Tong HC, Haig AJ, Yamakawa K. The Spurling test and cervical radiculopathy. Spine. 2002;27(2):156-159.

items.stem: Per Park et al., which finding-combination most raises the post-test probability of subacromial pathology?
options: Hawkins-Kennedy + painful arc + infraspinatus muscle test, all positive
Neer + drop arm, both positive
Any single positive impingement test
Night pain plus a positive Neer test
items.explanation: Park et al. found that combining the Hawkins-Kennedy, a painful arc, and the infraspinatus muscle test produced a positive likelihood ratio around 10 when all three were positive — a genuinely useful probability shift, where each test alone shifts probability only weakly. Clusters, not single tests, do the diagnostic work at the shoulder.
items.citation: Park HB, Yokota A, Gill HS, El Rassi G, McFarland EG. Diagnostic accuracy of clinical tests for the different degrees of subacromial impingement syndrome. J Bone Joint Surg Am. 2005;87(7):1446-1455.

items.stem: A 68-year-old presents with weakness and difficulty elevating the arm after a fall. You find a clear external rotation lag. Best interpretation?
options: A full-thickness cuff tear is now highly likely — discuss imaging/onward referral alongside rehab planning
This confirms subacromial impingement; begin a standard impingement program
A lag this size is normal age-related change
The result should be ignored until repeated on three separate visits
items.explanation: Near-perfect specificity means a clear lag is close to confirmatory, and this patient's age, trauma, and weakness made pretest probability high before you touched them — and sensitivity rises with tear extent, so a frank lag in this presentation suggests a substantial tear. High pretest + strongly specific positive = act on it. That doesn't automatically mean surgery — but it changes the conversation, the prognosis, and the rehab plan.
items.citation: Castoldi F, Blonna D, Hertel R. External rotation lag sign revisited. J Shoulder Elbow Surg. 2009;18(4):529-534 (Sn 56%/Sp 98% for full-thickness supraspinatus tear; sensitivity rises to ~97% for extensive tears); original description Hertel R, et al. J Shoulder Elbow Surg. 1996;5(4):307-313.

items.stem: A patient with anterolateral shoulder pain on overhead work has a negative Hawkins-Kennedy. How does this change your thinking?
options: It modestly lowers the probability of subacromial pain but cannot exclude it
Subacromial pain is now ruled out
The test result is meaningless in every direction
It confirms the pain is coming from the cervical spine
items.explanation: LR− ≈ 0.36 is a modest shift: if your pretest probability was 60%, a negative brings it down to roughly 35% — worth knowing, nowhere near exclusion. One moderately sensitive test never rules out a condition this common; the rest of the cluster and the history carry more weight.
items.citation: Hegedus EJ, et al. Br J Sports Med. 2012;46(14):964-978 (pooled estimates; LR− computed from pooled Sn/Sp).
items.contestedNote: Pooled estimates vary across meta-analyses and the impingement construct is disputed; treat the LR as approximate.

items.stem: Your pretest probability of subacromial pathology is about 50%. The Park cluster comes back fully positive (LR+ ≈ 10). Roughly what is the post-test probability?
options: Still 50% — likelihood ratios don't change probability
items.explanation: Pretest 50% = odds 1:1. Multiply by LR+ 10 → posttest odds 10:1 → probability 10/11 ≈ 91%. This is the whole trick of likelihood ratios: odds in, multiply, odds out. An LR of 10 is a big shift, but from 50% it still leaves ~9% uncertainty — not certainty.
items.pearl: Quick conversions worth memorizing: LR+ 2 ≈ +15 percentage points, LR+ 5 ≈ +30, LR+ 10 ≈ +45 (from mid-range pretest).
items.citation: LR+ from Park HB, et al. J Bone Joint Surg Am. 2005;87(7):1446-1455; Bayesian conversion is standard (e.g., McGee S. Evidence-Based Physical Diagnosis).

items.stem: The active compression (O'Brien) test was originally reported with sensitivity 100% and specificity 98.5% for labral pathology. Independent studies since have found far lower accuracy. What is the main lesson?
options: Accuracy reported by a test's developer is often the ceiling, not the truth — wait for independent replication
The original study must have contained fraudulent data
Later studies used the test incorrectly, so the original numbers stand
Labral pathology cannot exist if the test is inaccurate
items.explanation: Developer studies systematically overestimate accuracy: the inventors are unblinded experts, testing spectrum-biased populations, with flexible positive criteria. The O'Brien test is the textbook example — near-perfect in the original paper, mediocre in pooled independent data. Read the methods and who wrote them before trusting a sensitivity figure.
items.citation: O'Brien SJ, et al. The active compression test. Am J Sports Med. 1998;26(5):610-613; contrast pooled estimates in Hegedus EJ, et al. Br J Sports Med. 2012;46(14):964-978.
items.contestedNote: Reported accuracy for the O'Brien test ranges from near-perfect (original) to little better than chance (independent studies) — the disagreement is the teaching point.

items.stem: A 19-year-old rugby player, six weeks after a first-time dislocation, shows clear apprehension at 90° abduction with external rotation, easing with a relocation force. Interpretation?
options: Strongly supports anterior instability — structure the program around it and discuss recurrence risk
Non-specific finding; equally consistent with frozen shoulder
Rules out a labral lesion
Indicates cervical radiculopathy
items.explanation: High pretest probability (young, traumatic first dislocation) plus a highly specific positive (published LR 20.2 with the apprehension criterion) leaves little diagnostic doubt. The clinically useful conversation is now about recurrence risk — highest in exactly this demographic — and management options, not about whether instability exists.
items.citation: Farber AJ, et al. J Bone Joint Surg Am. 2006;88(7):1467-1474.

items.stem: In a patient whose history gives a LOW pretest probability of subacromial pain, the Hawkins-Kennedy comes back positive (Sp ~59%, LR+ ~1.9). The most defensible conclusion is:
options: There is a substantial chance this is a false positive — the probability has barely moved
Subacromial pathology is now the leading diagnosis
The patient should be referred for imaging to confirm impingement
Low pretest probability makes the positive result MORE convincing
items.explanation: A weak LR+ applied to a low pretest probability yields a still-low posttest probability — from 20% pretest, LR+ 1.9 gets you only to about 32%. Specificity of 59% means 4 of 10 patients without the condition also test positive. Positive findings in low-suspicion patients are where false positives live; this is the same logic that makes screening asymptomatic people with weak tests dangerous.
items.citation: Test properties from Hegedus EJ, et al. Br J Sports Med. 2012;46(14):964-978; probability arithmetic is standard Bayes.

items.stem: A shoulder patient's QuickDASH improves from 62 to 57 (5 points) over three weeks. Reported values for shoulder pain: MCID ≈ 8, MDC90 ≈ 11. What can you conclude?
options: Nothing firm — the change is below the MCID and within measurement error
The patient has meaningfully improved
The patient has meaningfully worsened
The questionnaire was scored incorrectly
items.explanation: Two separate bars, both unmet: 5 points is below the ~8-point MCID (too small to matter to patients) and below the ~11-point MDC90 (too small to distinguish from the instrument's own noise). The MDC is the stricter test here — a change inside it may not be real change at all. Keep treating and re-measure.
items.pearl: MDC asks 'is the change real?'; MCID asks 'does the change matter?'. A change must clear both to mean anything.
items.citation: Mintken PE, Glynn P, Cleland JA. Psychometric properties of the shortened Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder, and Hand Questionnaire (QuickDASH) and Numeric Pain Rating Scale in patients with shoulder pain. J Shoulder Elbow Surg. 2009;18(6):920-926.

items.stem: Published MCID estimates for the SPADI (Shoulder Pain and Disability Index) commonly range from about 8 to 13 points. How should a clinician handle that?
options: Treat the MCID as population- and method-specific — use the range, not one universal number
Always use 8, the smallest published value
Always use 13, the most conservative value
Discard the SPADI, since no single MCID exists
items.explanation: MCIDs are estimated against different anchors, timeframes, and populations, so a spread of values is expected, not a flaw. Practical use: changes below the whole range are unlikely to be meaningful, changes above it likely are, and changes inside it deserve judgment plus corroborating measures — rather than false precision from quoting one decimal. Note the reported minimal detectable change for repeated SPADI use is larger still (~18 points).
items.citation: Roy JS, MacDermid JC, Woodhouse LJ. Measuring shoulder function: a systematic review of four questionnaires. Arthritis Rheum. 2009;61(5):623-632.
items.contestedNote: SPADI MCID estimates genuinely vary across studies (~8–13+ points depending on population and anchor); no single value is authoritative.

items.stem: The MCID for the Numeric Pain Rating Scale has been reported as ~1.1 points in shoulder pain (Mintken) but ~2 points in low back pain (Childs). What does this tell you?
options: MCIDs are condition- and population-specific — a value validated in one population doesn't transfer automatically
Shoulder patients care less about pain than back patients
The NPRS is unreliable and should be abandoned
One of the two studies must be wrong
items.explanation: The same instrument can carry different MCIDs in different populations because the anchor ('are you meaningfully better?') behaves differently across conditions, baselines, and timeframes — Childs even reported different values at different follow-ups within the same LBP cohort (2.2 points at 1 week, 1.5 at 4 weeks). Quote the MCID for the population in front of you, and when none exists, say so rather than borrowing one silently.
items.citation: Mintken PE, et al. J Shoulder Elbow Surg. 2009;18(6):920-926 (shoulder); Childs JD, Piva SR, Fritz JM. Responsiveness of the numeric pain rating scale in patients with low back pain. Spine. 2005;30(11):1331-1334 (low back).

items.stem: What is the defining strength of the Patient-Specific Functional Scale (PSFS) — and its corresponding limitation?
options: Patients nominate their own meaningful activities, so it's highly relevant to the individual — but scores can't be compared between patients
It is the most reliable measure for comparing outcomes across a clinic's caseload
It eliminates the need for any region-specific outcome measure
It measures impairment rather than function
items.explanation: The PSFS asks the patient to name activities they can't do and rate each 0–10, which makes it exquisitely relevant to that person — the activities ARE the goals. The same feature means two patients' scores describe different activities, so between-patient or service-level comparison needs a standardized companion measure (e.g., QuickDASH or SPADI).
items.citation: Horn KK, Jennings S, Richardson G, Vliet DV, Hefford C, Abbott JH. The Patient-Specific Functional Scale: psychometrics, clinimetrics, and application as a clinical outcome measure. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther. 2012;42(1):30-42.

items.stem: Measuring shoulder external rotation with the arm at 90° of abduction, roughly what is the expected normal adult end-range?
items.explanation: Standard adult norms (AAOS values as tabulated in Norkin & White) put lateral rotation at about 90° when measured in 90° of abduction. Rotation measured with the arm at the side yields less. Norms vary with age, sport, and side — throwing athletes commonly show more ER and less IR on the dominant arm — so the contralateral shoulder is usually the more honest reference.
items.citation: Norkin CC, White DJ. Measurement of Joint Motion: A Guide to Goniometry. 5th ed. F.A. Davis; 2016 (AAOS normative values, shoulder lateral rotation).
